claims.title: Active interconnection queue, October 2026
claims.statement: The seven ISO/RTO queues (retrieved October 2026) plus LBNL data for non-ISO utilities contain 7,323 active requests totalling 1,686 GW.
method: Read each ISO's live queue and keep active requests. Per-ISO rules are in normalize_queues.py: SPP drops 'IA FULLY EXECUTED/COMMERCIAL OPERATION'; ERCOT drops projects already approved for synchronisation (they are in EIA's operating fleet); PJM keeps Active, Confirmed, Engineering and Procurement, Suspended, Under Construction and Partially in Service.
MW per request = the ISO's injection or net-to-grid figure (CAISO 'Net MWs to Grid', PJM 'MFO', NYISO 'SP (MW)', ERCOT 'Capacity (MW)', MISO/SPP/ISO-NE the largest MW field).
Add LBNL active requests for regions 'West' and 'Southeast' (utilities outside ISOs, end-2025).
For CAISO, MISO, NYISO, PJM and ISO-NE, whose live files also list withdrawn or completed requests, add LBNL active requests whose ID never appears in the live file (e.g. CAISO Cluster 15).
Drop requests with missing or non-positive MW, then duplicate ISO:ID pairs.
Count rows and sum MW: 7,323 requests, 1,685,552.9 MW.
claims.caveats: Mixed vintages: ISO data is from October 2026, non-ISO utilities are LBNL end-2025. Hybrids are counted once at their injection limit, so the total is not comparable with LBNL's separate generation + storage figures (1,312 GW + 749 GW).

claims.title: LBNL dataset: requests by status
claims.statement: The LBNL Queued Up data file (through end-2025) lists 38,201 requests: 8,513 active and 24,221 withdrawn.

sources.name: LBNL Queued Up (2026 ed.)
sources.detail: sheet '03. Complete Queue Data', columns q_id, q_status, mw_1

method: Load every row of the project-level sheet (all years, all statuses).
Group by q_status; count rows and sum mw_1 (capacity of the main resource type).
claims.caveats: LBNL's report cites about 8,200 active projects and 1,312 GW generation + 749 GW storage. Those are its own cleaned figures and are quoted, not recomputed here. The data file marks more rows as active.

claims.title: Most requests never get built
claims.statement: Of 19,779 requests that entered a queue in 2000–2019, 4,015 (20.3%) reached commercial operation and 14,088 (71.2%) withdrew. By capacity, 13.9% of the requested MW was built.

sources.name: LBNL Queued Up (2026 ed.)
sources.detail: sheet '03. Complete Queue Data', columns q_year, q_status, mw_1

method: Load the project-level sheet.
Keep rows whose q_year (year the request entered the queue) is 2000–2019 inclusive: 19,779 rows (665 rows without q_year excluded).
Operational share = rows with q_status 'operational' ÷ all kept rows = 4,015 ÷ 19,779.
Withdrawn share = rows with q_status 'withdrawn' ÷ all kept rows = 14,088 ÷ 19,779.
Repeat by 5-year cohort (table).
claims.caveats: Counts requests, not MW. The 2015–19 cohort still has active requests that may yet be built or withdraw, so its final completion rate is not settled. 2020+ cohorts are excluded for that reason.

claims.title: New interconnection requests per year
claims.statement: Between 2,323 and 3,435 new requests entered US queues each year in 2019–2025.

sources.name: LBNL Queued Up (2026 ed.)
sources.detail: sheet '03. Complete Queue Data', columns q_year, q_id, mw_1

method: Load the project-level sheet (all statuses: requests that later withdrew still count as filed).
Group by q_year; count rows and sum mw_1.
claims.caveats: 2025 may be slightly undercounted if some requests were added to queues after LBNL's data cut-off.

claims.title: Transmission providers in the queue data
claims.statement: The LBNL data covers 57 distinct transmission-provider entities (54 with active requests).

sources.name: LBNL Queued Up (2026 ed.)
sources.detail: sheet '03. Complete Queue Data', columns entity, region, q_status

method: Count distinct values of 'entity' (transmission provider: ISO or utility), overall and among active requests.
claims.caveats: Each ISO counts as one entity even though it covers many transmission owners.

claims.title: Developers named in the active queue
claims.statement: Only 33% of 8,513 active requests name a developer, and those show 1,871 distinct developer names (359 with 2+ requests, 41 with 5+).

sources.name: LBNL Queued Up (2026 ed.)
sources.detail: sheet '03. Complete Queue Data', columns developer, q_status, region

method: Keep active requests.
Drop empty developer fields ('nan', 'unknown', 'n/a', 'not available').
Normalise names: lower-case; remove LLC, Inc, LP, Corp, Corporation, Company, Co, Ltd; remove commas and full stops.
Count distinct normalised names and requests per name.
claims.caveats: Many names are project-specific companies (one LLC per project), so parent developers are fewer than the distinct names. Several ISOs publish no developer names at all, so the national count is uncertain.

claims.title: Requests still in study
claims.statement: 4,646 of the 7,323 active requests (1,148 GW) have not yet signed an interconnection agreement.
method: Start from the active-queue table of C1.
Each ISO's status is mapped to four phases in normalize_queues.py (e.g. MISO DPP Phase 2/3 → late study; PJM 'Engineering and Procurement' → IA executed; NYISO status codes 10–11 → IA executed).
Group by phase; count requests and sum MW.
claims.caveats: ISO-NE publishes no study phase, so its requests are counted as early study.

claims.title: How queue requests were placed on the map
claims.statement: 46% of requests are placed by matching their point-of-interconnection name to a substation; 51% by county proximity only.

sources.name: OpenStreetMap substations + HIFLD line endpoint labels

method: Geocode each request's county (Census boundaries; LBNL FIPS where available).

Clean the POI text (remove kV, 'substation', bus numbers, …) and fuzzy-match it (score ≥ 87) to named substations within 150 km of the county, favouring matching voltage and proximity. 'Line endpoint' means the POI named a line (A–B) and one end matched.
Otherwise place it at the nearest substation of plausible voltage to the county centre.
Requests with neither county nor matchable name stay unlocated.
claims.caveats: County-proximity placements are right in aggregate but can be wrong for an individual project.

claims.title: Size of the network model
claims.statement: The power-flow model solves 29,170 buses and 41,484 lines in three interconnections for two scenarios; building network, queue matching, model and map export took 6 minutes on a laptop (data/rebuild.log).
method: Count buses and lines inside the three main connected networks (islands excluded).
Runtime = first to last timestamp in data/rebuild.log (steps 4–7 of the pipeline; downloads excluded).
claims.caveats: Runtime depends on the machine; downloads (≈1 hour, mostly OpenStreetMap) are not included.

claims.title: Substations with room for new generation
claims.statement: Of 16,674 named, modelled substations at 115 kV or above, 27% are green, 45% are yellow, 28% are red.
method: Keep buses in the three modelled networks, with a name, at ≥ 115 kV.
Signal: green ≥ 250 MW of generation headroom after the queue; yellow 75–250 MW; red < 75 MW or queued MW > 1.5 × the substation's N-1 branch capacity.
Count by signal.
claims.caveats: Screening model: estimated ratings, no N-1 contingency analysis (see README limitations).

claims.title: Congestion where projects are queued, by region
claims.statement: Among named substations at ≥ 115 kV that host queued requests, the share rated red differs sharply by region.
method: Keep named, modelled substations at ≥ 115 kV with at least one queued request.
Assign each substation the region (ISO, or LBNL 'West'/'Southeast') that most of its queued requests come from.
Per region: share of substations with a red signal, and median generation headroom after the queue.
claims.caveats: Screening model; a region's red share also reflects how large its queue is.

claims.title: Lines holding back the queue (reconductoring candidates)
claims.statement: 413 line segments (18,864 km) set the limit for substations holding 914 GW of queued requests. Of these, 338 are limited by heat rather than stability and shorter than 80 km (8,179 km, 673 GW behind), the lines where new conductors add capacity.
method: For every substation, the model records which line sets its generation headroom after the queue (the binding constraint).
'Queued MW behind' a line = total queued MW at the substations whose limit is that line. Each substation is counted once, so totals do not double count.
Keep lines with ≥ 500 MW behind them; then those whose screening limit is thermal (not the St. Clair stability limit) and that are ≤ 80 km long.
claims.caveats: Screening model. Many queued MW sit at substations placed by county proximity (C8), and line names come from HIFLD endpoint labels.

claims.title: Storage and reconductoring candidate substations
claims.statement: 735 modelled buses have under 100 MW of generation headroom after the queue but at least 150 MW of solar and wind behind them.
method: Renewables behind a bus = existing solar + wind at the bus (EIA-860M) + 30% of its queued MW.
Candidate if modelled, headroom after queue < 100 MW and renewables behind ≥ 150 MW.
claims.caveats: The 30% share of queued MW and both thresholds are screening assumptions.

claims.title: Market sizing arithmetic (TAM / SAM / SOM)
claims.statement: With the stated assumptions, the US market is about $96.8M a year (TAM), $64.6M serviceable (SAM), and $4.3M of recurring revenue plausibly won by year 5 (SOM).

sources.name: Counts from C4, C5, C6; prices are hypotheses

method: Developers: 1,200 organisations (C6 shows 1,871 names, many project LLCs) × weighted price (70% × $15k + 25% × $50k + 5% × $150k = $30.5k).
Data centers 300 × $100k; investors & off-takers 400 × $40k; utilities 57 (C5) × $250k.
SAM drops the largest developers, 30% of data-center demand and all utilities.
SOM = named account targets for year 5.
Cross-check: new requests per year (C4) × 5 sites screened × $1,000 per report.
claims.caveats: Only the organisation counts for utilities (C5) and the developer signal (C4, C6) come from data. All prices, the data-center and investor counts, and the SAM/SOM shares are assumptions to test in interviews.

claims.title: Spot checks at well-known substations
claims.statement: Model values at substations named in our discussion, for comparison with what is known about them.
method: Look up each name among modelled substations; where a name repeats, take the highest-voltage one.
claims.caveats: Values at or near 3,000 MW are the display cap: big 500 kV hubs read too high because transformer limits and contingencies are not modelled.

claims.title: Size of the input datasets
claims.statement: Record counts of the main physical-grid inputs.
method: Count features / rows in each downloaded file (generators: operating or standby units in the contiguous US; capacity = net summer MW).

rows: all US incl. AK/HI; 51,861 AC segments in CONUS used

claims.title: Odds that a queued request gets built, by region and stage
claims.statement: Of 18,103 requests filed 2000–2019 that have since been built or withdrawn, 22% were built overall, and 60% of those that signed an interconnection agreement (IA) were built. The map weights every active request by these odds for its region and stage.

sources.name: LBNL Queued Up (2026 ed.)
sources.detail: sheet '03. Complete Queue Data', columns q_year, q_status, ia_date, IA_phase_clean, region

method: Keep requests that entered a queue in 2000–2019 and are now 'operational' (built) or 'withdrawn'.
A request 'reached an IA' if it has an IA date or LBNL marks it 'IA Executed' (LBNL marks all built projects this way).

IA-executed odds = built ÷ requests that reached an IA. Early-study odds = share that reached an IA × IA-executed odds. Late-study odds = midpoint of the two (assumption: LBNL does not record the stage at which withdrawn requests left). Under construction = 90% (assumption).
Regional values are shrunk towards the national value with the weight of 50 requests.
claims.caveats: Survivorship: the 2000–2019 cohorts reflect older queue rules. Since FERC Order 2023, deposits and readiness rules may raise completion rates for today's requests.
used_in: Atlas: queue weights and risk assessment

claims.title: How long interconnection takes, by region
claims.statement: Projects that came online 2018–2025 took a median 4.4 years from request to operation; interconnection agreements signed 2020–2025 took a median 2.7 years from request.

sources.name: LBNL Queued Up (2026 ed.)
sources.detail: sheet '03. Complete Queue Data', columns q_date, ia_date, on_date, region

method: Request → operation: built projects with an online date in 2018–2025; years = online date − queue date (0–25 years kept).
Request → agreement: requests with an IA date in 2020–2025; years = IA date − queue date (0–20 kept).
Report median and 25th–75th percentile per region; regions with fewer than 20 cases fall back to national.
claims.caveats: Only completed projects count, so slow projects still in the queue are missing: true durations for today's applicants are likely longer.

claims.title: What interconnection studies actually cost
claims.statement: LBNL's cost datasets cover 4,713 studied projects in MISO, PJM, SPP, NYISO, ISO-NE and five non-ISO balancing authorities; 97% are placed on a substation of our network.

sources.name: LBNL interconnection costs (MISO)

method: Read each file; for the non-ISO file keep the latest study per project.
Convert ISO costs from 2022 to 2024 dollars with the CPI-U annual-average ratio 313.689 / 292.655 = 1.072.
Place ISO projects on a bus by joining their queue ID to the located LBNL history; place non-ISO projects at the nearest bus within 15 km of their published POI coordinates.
Medians by region (all study years and statuses).
claims.caveats: Costs are those assigned in studies, not final costs; withdrawn projects (often the most expensive) are included because a new applicant faces the same study. CAISO and ERCOT are not covered.

claims.title: Does the map's congestion signal match real study costs?
claims.statement: Across 3,191 studies since 2018 placed on modelled substations, projects at substations the map colours red were assigned a median $63/kW of network upgrades, versus $36/kW at green ones (1.7×). Costs also rise with project size relative to the modelled headroom.

sources.name: Cost studies on buses + model buses

method: Keep cost studies from 2018 on that sit on a modelled substation.
Group by the substation's generation signal today and compare median network-upgrade cost.
Group by project MW ÷ modelled existing-grid headroom. The multipliers in brackets (median of cost ÷ regional median) are what the risk model applies; voltage multipliers likewise.
claims.caveats: Today's grid model is compared with studies done 2018–2023, while the grid and queue changed in between. It shows a directional relationship, not a precise prediction.

claims.title: Bigger upgrades, longer waits
claims.statement: Built projects in MISO, PJM and SPP (queued 2010 or later) with under $10/kW of network upgrades took a median 2.4 years from request to operation; those with over $150/kW took 3.9 years.
method: Keep cost-study projects with a queue date (2010+) and an in-service date; years = in-service − queue (0.3–20).
Group by network-upgrade cost tier; multiplier = tier median ÷ overall median. The risk model multiplies the regional time-to-operation by the multiplier of the expected cost tier.
claims.caveats: Small samples in the top tier; NYISO, ISO-NE and non-ISO files have no in-service dates.

claims.title: How risk grades are distributed
claims.value: share of substations by grade and project size
claims.statement: With default weights, most substations earn A or B for a 50 MW project, while most earn D or E for 1,000 MW.
method: Cost score: 100 at $25/kW falling linearly to 0 at $400/kW. Time score: 100 at 2.5 years to 0 at 8.0 years. Capacity score = chance the project still fits (0–100).
Risk index = 100 − (35% cost + 30% time + 35% capacity). Grades: A < 25, B 25–40, C 40–55, D 55–70, E ≥ 70.
Capacity fit allows a log-normal error of σ = 0.5 on the modelled headroom (assumption).
claims.caveats: The anchors, weights and model-error allowance are judgement calls, not data; they decide the grade boundaries.

claims.title: Unit costs used to price upgrades
claims.statement: Substation connections and line upgrades are priced with MISO's exploratory unit costs (2024 dollars, including 30% contingency and financing during construction).
method: Connection = 'add 1 position, breaker-and-a-half bus' at the substation's highest voltage.
Line upgrade = reconductor if the line is heat-limited and the needed extra flow is at most its usable rating; otherwise a new single-circuit line (median of MISO's state values).
Cost per mile × line length; the project's share = its added flow ÷ (its added flow + the queue's overload).
claims.caveats: MISO's figures are planning estimates for its footprint; costs elsewhere (e.g. California, the Northeast) are typically higher. Reconductoring with advanced conductors costs more than the ACSR/ACSS basis.

claims.title: What predicts that a project reaches operation
claims.statement: Among 18,099 requests filed 2000–2019 that were built or withdrawn, the tenth our model rates lowest was 9% built and the tenth it rates highest 49%. Discrimination (AUC) is 0.67 in 5-fold cross-validation, against 0.58 for region alone (what the map's queue weights use).

sources.name: LBNL Queued Up (2026 ed.)
sources.detail: sheet '03. Complete Queue Data', columns q_year, q_status, IA_phase_clean, ia_date, type_clean, mw_1-3, region, fips_code, poi_name, q_date

method: Keep requests filed 2000–2019. Built = 1, withdrawn = 0; the 1,662 still active count fractionally with their region × stage odds (C17).

Features known at filing: region, technology, size, POI voltage, other requests in the same county and technology filed within 60 days (parallel filings), the county's NREL siting ordinance (restrictive = ban, project-size cap, or setback ≥ 2,000 ft for wind / ≥ 500 ft for solar from non-participating homes), entry era.
Regularised logistic regression (L2 = 1). A second fit on requests that signed an interconnection agreement (7,895) scores projects past that stage; late study takes the midpoint.
Coefficients are centred on the training mix, so ×1.00 = typical; the page shows each as percentage points.
Out-of-time check: trained on 2000–2014 filings, AUC 0.60 on 2015–2019; it predicted 25% built against 19% resolved so far.

rows: Same county & technology filed within 60 days
Same county & technology filed within 60 days
Same county & technology filed within 60 days

claims.caveats: Public attributes explain only part of the outcome; site control, financing and offtake are not in the data. Service type (NRIS/ERIS) and the proposed online date were left out: regions record them inconsistently, and LBNL stores the latest proposed date, which leaks the outcome. The ordinance data was extracted with LLMs by NREL and most ordinances post-date the 2000–2019 filings.

claims.title: Expensive studies end in withdrawal
claims.statement: Of 2,883 studied requests that were later built or withdrawn, 63% of those assigned under $10/kW of network upgrades were built, against 3% of those assigned over $400/kW. The score uses the developer's own study cost when given.

method: Keep cost-study projects whose status is Withdrawn, Complete or Operational and that have a network cost.
Built share by network-cost tier.
Logistic regression built ~ cost tier + region; tier coefficients centred on the tier mix (odds column). Applied only before an interconnection agreement is signed.
claims.caveats: Cost is known only after a study, so it applies to projects already studied. ERCOT and CAISO are not covered.

claims.title: Permitted projects get built more often
claims.statement: Of planned units on EIA's December 2021 list, 32% of those whose regulatory approvals had not started were operating by the current file, against 49% of those with approvals received.
method: Planned units of at least 5 MW in December 2021, by status code: (P) approvals not initiated = Not started, (L) approvals pending = Applied, (T) approvals received = Approved.
Built = the same plant and generator ID appears as operating (or since retired) in the current file.
Odds ratio against Not started; the score adds its log as a driver.
claims.caveats: EIA's planned list holds projects close to construction, not early queue requests, and the sample is small.

claims.title: Score inputs that are assumptions
claims.statement: No public dataset links local opposition or offtake contracts to queue outcomes. Until users' outcomes calibrate them, the score applies these team estimates (marked * on the page).
method: Each answer multiplies the odds of reaching operation by the factor shown.
Under construction is scored at 90%, as in the map's queue weights (C17).
Remaining time under construction is taken as 0.5–2 years.
claims.caveats: Judgement, not data. County ordinance data (C24) shows only a small effect in public records, so project-specific opposition is left to the developer's answer.
